subject: maths
title: Decimals — place value and operations

slides.heading: Place value — what each digit is worth
slides.body: The position of each digit tells you its value: the 1st digit after the decimal point is tenths (÷10), the 2nd is hundredths (÷100), the 3rd is thousandths (÷1000). This is why 0.3 and 0.03 are very different numbers — the digit 3 sits in different columns.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: Multiplying decimals — the digit-count method
slides.formula: Multiply as integers → count total decimal places → insert decimal point
slides.formulaExplained: Multiply the numbers ignoring the decimal points. Then count how many decimal places appear in the original numbers combined — that is exactly how many decimal places the answer must have. Place the decimal point that many positions from the right of your integer product.
slides.whenToUse: Every time you multiply two decimal numbers together — it avoids having to convert to fractions first.
slides.note: Show formula in standard notation. Explain each variable. State when this formula applies.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: Calculate 4.7 × 2.3.

steps.instruction: Multiply as whole numbers, ignoring the decimal points.
Count the total decimal places in the original numbers.
steps.working: 4.7 has 1 d.p. and 2.3 has 1 d.p. Total = 2 decimal places.

steps.instruction: Place the decimal point 2 positions from the right of 1081.

steps.working: 4.7 ≈ 5 and 2.3 ≈ 2, so the answer should be close to 10. 10.81 is reasonable.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Misaligning decimal points when adding — e.g. writing 3.6 + 0.48 as 3.6 + 0.48 with the digits lined up by position count rather than decimal point, giving 1.08 instead of 4.08.
mistakes.correction: Always align the decimal points in a column first: 3.60 + 0.48 = 4.08. Adding a trailing zero (3.60) makes the alignment obvious.

mistakes.mistake: Counting only one number's decimal places when multiplying — e.g. computing 3.2 × 1.4: multiplying 32 × 14 = 448, then placing only 1 decimal place to get 44.8 instead of the correct 4.48.
mistakes.correction: Count decimal places in both numbers and add them together. 3.2 (1 d.p.) × 1.4 (1 d.p.) → total 2 d.p. → 4.48.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking 0.3 × 0.4 = 1.2 by treating the digits as whole-number multiplication — forgetting that tenths × tenths = hundredths.
mistakes.correction: 0.3 × 0.4: integers 3 × 4 = 12, total 2 d.p. → 0.12. Multiplying two numbers less than 1 always gives a smaller result.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: Place value: 1st decimal digit = tenths (÷10), 2nd = hundredths (÷100), 3rd = thousandths (÷1000).
keyFacts.examTip: If you confuse tenths and hundredths, your decimal will be out by a factor of 10 — a very common error.

keyFacts.fact: To add or subtract decimals, always align the decimal points before calculating. Insert trailing zeros (e.g. 3.6 → 3.60) to make columns clear.
keyFacts.examTip: Draw a vertical line at the decimal point position and check every digit sits in the correct column.

keyFacts.fact: To multiply decimals: multiply as integers, then count the total decimal places across both numbers and place the decimal point that many positions from the right.
keyFacts.examTip: Use an estimate to check — if 4.7 × 2.3 ≈ 5 × 2 = 10, then 10.81 makes sense and 108.1 does not.
